title: Prohibition liquor and the Shreveport policeman
summary: Under Ed Williams the band's musicians keep their own whiskey in the leader's house; Love tells how a Shreveport policeman made him drink his pint as evidence.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: He brought that in there. But shortly after that, man, they passed the city ordinance. He couldn't bring no liquor in Sreeport, not over a court. Like, you got a coronet or something like that, a detective get on there and say, you got liquor in there? No, sir. Open it up. He opened it up, you know. I said, I got a court in there. Where you get that Monroe? All right, they lie to have a court. That was during Prohibition though. Yeah. If they catch you with any more than that though, yeah.
Tell where you got it from or go to jail.

Ed Williams was a sharp fellow, the fellow who was the leader of the band. He had a big house with all the musicians, just a room there with him. He'd give parties, you know. And he had that liquor hidden around there. See like I lived there, I'd order me a court from Monroe. That's mine, you see. When he'd come I'd give it to him, see. The guitar player, he'd order a court. He'd come and give it to Ed. All of us have our own whiskey, you know. You'd have about seven eight quarts of whiskey in the same house. They never did look for it or nothing like that. They know we were musicians and they'd like to have a court. But a funny thing one night though, they caught me with a pint of the lid and they'd have a pint of liquor on Texas Avenue. They'd pass the city ordinance if you have any liquor like that you had to drink it up. If you didn't drink it up, they'd put you in jail. And if you'd drink it up and got drunk, they'd put you in jail. The police would have caught me, you know. And I had been drinking but I didn't have a whole pint, about a half a pint in a pint, you see. Searched me. Grab against that plant. I got up. Searched me. What's that? You got liquor, huh? I said, where'd you get that from? I said, it come from Monroe. I said, you know. Well, you know, you got to drink up that evidence. I was pretty high then, you know. I didn't want no more. I just had it in my pocket, you know. You see, you got to drink up the evidence if you don't. What you got left, that's the evidence against you. I'm going to arrest you. I said, all right, sir. Give me a little time. I took the bottle out, you know. He said, go ahead, start on. I said, nipped it a little bit and looked at it, you know. He said, uh-uh. Get busy. I said, get busy. I said, all right. I said, I don't think I can drink all. I'll have to rest. I said, well, if I drink it all, you ain't going to rest me? He said, no, I'll let you go if you drink it all. I looked at it again, you know. I said, I'm going to carry it all the way this time. Gluck, gluck. I said, throw that bottle out there. I said, you sure can drink. You can drink some liquor. I said, now get on off. I said, if you don't walk straight, I'm going to put you in anyhow, you know. And I buttoned my coat up, good, you know, like that. Pulled my hat off, you know, and started off kind of slow, you know. I said, good night, Cap. Man, I started to run, and I had to run. I couldn't walk straight. I'd have done that way. I said, good night, Cap. And when I got way down on Sprague Street, you know, I heard him laughing. Quack, quack, quack. I was laughing to keep from falling, you know. I was running to keep from falling. I said, oh, tickle that policeman. He seen me the next day, he said, I don't want to catch you with no more liquor now. I said, you can drink some liquor, Sam. I'm going to put you in jail if I see you with him. They would stick around there.
